    Why it's here: 13 weeks old; 12 citations
    source
  8. Align AI and Mathematics—to Something Else — Bits of DNA (Lior Pachter) · Worth reading

    Why it's here: 9 days old; 34 Hacker News points / 47 comments
    source

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Monday, September 21st. Today we trace a line from decades-old basic science finally reaching patients, to fast-moving artificial intelligence reshaping biology, medicine, and even mathematics itself.

We start with narcolepsy. The New York Times reports that a new drug is offering relief to people living with this debilitating sleep disorder. According to the paper's summary, it's described as a first-of-its-kind treatment, though the available reporting doesn't specify its mechanism or trial data in detail. This item made the cut because it connects directly to our next story, which explains where this drug actually came from.

That's the Lasker Award, one of the most prestigious prizes in biomedical science. The New York Times reports that two researchers who study narcolepsy have won this year's award. Their research, conducted in animals, identified the root cause of the condition, and that discovery laid the groundwork for the new drug we just described. It's a tidy example of how basic research in animal models can take decades to translate into a treatment that reaches actual patients, but eventually does.

Staying with the heart, but jumping to fundamental pharmacology, a new paper in Science addresses a long-standing puzzle about one of the most widely used classes of heart failure drugs: SGLT2 inhibitors. These drugs produce strong benefits for patients, but researchers have not been sure how, since the benefits appear to happen independently of their known target, a glucose transporter called SGLT2. The authors, led by Nicholas Forelli at the Cardiovascular Institute of the South and the University of Pennsylvania, report finding a different target entirely: an enzyme called pantothenate kinase 1, which kicks off the process of converting vitamin B5 into coenzyme A, a molecule that essentially every fuel-burning pathway in heart cells depends on. Using stable isotope tracing and experiments on donated human heart tissue, including hearts from patients with heart failure, the team showed that these drugs directly bind and activate this enzyme, restoring low coenzyme A levels seen in failing hearts and broadly boosting the heart's ability to burn fuel. They also used computer modeling to map where on the enzyme the drug binds, and found that blocking this enzyme cancels out the drug's ability to increase contraction in isolated human heart cells. This is a peer-reviewed paper using human heart tissue and cell experiments, and it has drawn sixteen citations in about four weeks, a sign the cardiology field is paying close attention to what may be the real explanation for these drugs' clinical benefits.

Next, a computational biology paper in Nature proposes something the authors call a universal cell embedding, essentially a foundation model for cell biology. A team led by Yanay Rosen at Stanford trained this model on a huge amount of single-cell data using self-supervised learning, a technique that doesn't require researchers to label the data beforehand. The result is a shared mathematical space that can represent cells from many different tissues and species at once. The authors used it to build what they call the Integrated Mega-scale Atlas, embedding 36 million cells covering more than a thousand distinct cell types across eight species. They report that the model shows what they call emergent behavior, meaning it appears to pick up on biological patterns, like developmental relationships between cell types, that it was never explicitly trained to detect, and it can even represent data from species it never saw during training. This is a peer-reviewed paper, and with twelve citations in eleven weeks, it's being recognized as a resource other researchers can build on for analysis and hypothesis generation, though as with any single model, how well it generalizes to entirely new biological questions will be tested over time.

From cells in general to cancer immunotherapy specifically, a paper in Nature Medicine introduces a model the authors call Compass, designed to predict which cancer patients will respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors. This matters because these drugs are now standard treatment across many cancer types, yet most patients don't respond, and existing biomarkers don't generalize well across different tumors and drugs. The team, led by Wan Xiang Shen at Harvard University, Zhejiang University, and the Broad Institute, trained their model on gene expression data from over ten thousand tumors spanning thirty-three cancer types. Rather than treating the model as a black box, they built it around forty-four biological concepts, things like immune cell states and specific signaling pathways, so its predictions can be traced back to identifiable biology. Tested against twenty-two existing methods across sixteen independent patient groups covering seven cancers and six different checkpoint inhibitor drugs, the authors report their model improved prediction accuracy by about eight and a half percent. In survival analysis, patients the model identified as likely responders lived substantially longer than those it flagged as non-responders. The authors also used the model to explore why some patients don't respond even when their tumors appear immune-active, pointing to factors like a signaling pathway called TGF-beta and a lack of certain immune cell types. This is a peer-reviewed paper with sixteen citations in under three months, reflecting real interest in a tool that could help design future immunotherapy trials, though it will need prospective clinical testing before it changes practice.

Now to a story that's less about a single result and more about a controversy roiling the mathematics and AI communities. A letter titled "A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics," reportedly signed initially by twenty-five Fields Medalists, mathematics' highest honor, has generated enormous discussion online, drawing more than twelve hundred points and over twelve hundred comments on the tech forum Hacker News. We only have the headline for this item, so we can't detail its specific arguments here, but its scale of engagement alone signals a real rift over how AI companies are approaching mathematical research.

That rift gets a direct response from computational biologist Lior Pachter, writing on his blog Bits of DNA. Pachter agrees with the Fields Medalists that AI companies' rushed announcements, apparently including one from OpenAI regarding the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a famous open question in fluid dynamics, undercut the kind of careful, attributed work mathematics is supposed to value. But he argues the mathematics community itself has a poor track record of, in his words, nurturing students and ideas with care. He walks through historical cases: a mathematician denied academic refuge before being murdered in the Holocaust, a researcher passed over for a Fields Medal despite foundational contributions to the very equations later cited by the AI announcement, and more recent accounts of discrimination and poor mentorship within university mathematics departments. Pachter's conclusion is that neither AI companies nor the mathematics establishment should be the standard to align to. Instead, he suggests both should be judged against values like understanding, proper attribution, and genuinely nurturing new ideas and the people producing them. This essay drew thirty-four points and forty-seven comments on Hacker News, modest by comparison, but notable as a working scientist's direct engagement with the bigger controversy.

We'll close with a story that has nothing to do with AI at all. A paper in Nature reports isotopic measurements of 3I ATLAS, an interstellar comet, meaning an object that formed around another star before passing through our solar system. A team led by Martin Cordiner at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, along with colleagues at the University of America and Northern Arizona University, measured the ratios of hydrogen and carbon isotopes in the comet's water and carbon-based gases. They found the water is enriched in deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen, at a level more than ten times higher than in any known comet from our own solar system. The carbon isotope ratios also fell outside the typical range seen in our solar system or in nearby star-forming regions. The authors say these extreme signatures point to formation at extremely cold temperatures, below thirty degrees above absolute zero, in an environment relatively poor in heavier elements. Using models of how our galaxy's chemistry has changed over time, they estimate the comet may have formed as long as twelve billion years ago, during an early, intense period of star formation. This is a peer-reviewed paper with twelve citations in thirteen weeks, offering a rare direct chemical sample of how planetary building blocks form around stars very different from our own.

That's your briefing for today. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back tomorrow with more.

    Why it's here: 16 days old; 773 Hacker News points / 512 comments

    Scientists used genome language models to generate viable bacteriophage genomes capable of overcoming resistant E. coli.
    Why it's here: 6 weeks old; 6 citations
    source

    404 Media found that a company advertising '100% human-written' medical research relied on AI-generated staff and content.

  9. LLMs as a Cognitive Virus — arxiv.org · Worth reading
    A preprint models the spread of large language model use as a viral process that could lead to cognitive dependence or immunization.
    Why it's here: 15 days old; 398 Hacker News points / 256 comments
    source · Hacker News discussion

Transcript

Welcome to your science briefing for Sunday, September 20. Today we cover a personalized cancer vaccine trial, a genome-scale map of T cell regulation, an AI that designed working virus genomes, and a set of stories about how artificial intelligence is reshaping trust in science and mathematics itself.

We start with oncology. Moderna and Merck announced positive results from a Phase 3 trial called INTerpath-001, testing an individualized messenger RNA therapy named intismeran autogene alongside the drug Keytruda in patients with resected stage two-B through four melanoma. According to the companies, the trial met its primary endpoint of recurrence-free survival and a key secondary endpoint of distant metastasis-free survival. This is described as the first positive Phase 3 result for a personalized neoantigen therapy, and the first for any messenger RNA-based cancer treatment. It's worth noting this news comes from a company announcement posted on social media, not yet a published peer-reviewed paper, so details like actual survival numbers and statistical significance aren't available yet. Still, it drew more than six hundred points and around three hundred comments on Hacker News, reflecting how significant the field considers this milestone, since these vaccines are custom-built for each patient's specific tumor mutations.

Next, a foundational immunology paper from researchers at the Gladstone Institutes and collaborators, published in the journal Cell. The team perturbed nearly every expressed gene across twenty-two million primary human CD4 positive T cells, taken from four donors, using a technique called Perturb-seq. This is a peer-reviewed cell-based study, not an animal or human trial. The authors report they mapped genes that regulate T cell behavior both at rest and after stimulation, identifying new regulators of cytokine production and factors involved in T helper cell polarization and age-related changes in T cells. They also linked some of these context-specific regulatory pathways to autoimmune disease risk. The paper has picked up seventeen citations in about seven weeks, suggesting researchers are already building on this resource to study human immune function.

Moving to diagnostics, the FDA has cleared a blood test called PrecivityAD2 for marketing, developed by C2N Diagnostics, a company that grew out of research at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. The test uses high-resolution mass spectrometry to measure amyloid and tau protein levels in blood, biomarkers linked to the plaques associated with Alzheimer's disease. According to the university's report, previous studies found the test could identify amyloid pathology with more than ninety percent accuracy, performing comparably to spinal taps and brain scans, including in patients with mild symptoms. FDA clearance means the test can now be marketed more broadly and may be more easily covered by insurance. This is a diagnostic milestone rather than a new treatment, but the researchers note that existing Alzheimer's drugs work better when started early, which is why easier detection matters. The story generated about one hundred ninety points and over one hundred comments on Hacker News.

In genomics, researchers including scientists from the University of Pennsylvania and Google published a global survey of human centromeres in Nature. Centromeres are the highly repetitive regions of chromosomes essential for cell division, and they've historically been difficult to sequence completely. The authors assembled and characterized over two thousand one hundred complete centromeres from a diverse group of individuals spanning five continental and twenty-eight population groups. They report finding hundreds of previously unknown centromere variants, and observed that mobile genetic elements appear in about thirty percent of centromeres. They also found that mutation rates vary fifty-fold across different chromosomes, with the region where the cell's division machinery attaches, called the kinetochore site, mutating fastest of all. The authors describe this as evidence of an evolutionary arms race between centromeric DNA and the proteins that bind it. This peer-reviewed paper has drawn nine citations in eight weeks.

Staying with AI applied to biology, a paper in Science introduces Biomni, described by its authors at Stanford and Sunesis as a general-purpose artificial intelligence agent for biomedical research. The system mines tools, databases, and protocols from thousands of publications, then autonomously plans and executes research tasks such as prioritizing disease-causing genes, drug repurposing, and rare-disease diagnosis, without needing task-specific training. The authors report case studies in which the system interpreted complex datasets, helped optimize protein stability, and generated testable experimental protocols. This is a peer-reviewed computational paper describing a software agent, not a clinical result. It has accumulated eleven citations in ten weeks.

Now to mathematics, and a story that generated enormous discussion. Anthropic reports that its Claude model produced what it calls the first complete, computer-checked proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, written in the formal proof language Lean. According to Anthropic, Claude worked largely autonomously over eleven days, producing thirteen million lines of Lean code and proving about twenty-nine thousand five hundred intermediate theorems, following a known mathematical route to the proof rather than discovering new mathematics. Mathematician Kevin Buzzard, who has led a multi-year community effort on this formalization, reviewed the result and called it an extraordinary achievement, though he noted it should be checked further. It's important to be precise here: this is a company report, not an independent peer-reviewed verification, and the achievement is about automatically translating and checking an existing proof, not discovering a new one. Even so, it touched off substantial debate, drawing over seven hundred points and more than five hundred comments on Hacker News, with discussion centered on what it means for trust in mathematical proofs going forward.

Back to biology, but now the engineering side. Researchers from the Arc Research Institute, Stanford, and the Palo Alto Institute report in Science what they call the first generative design of complete bacteriophage genomes using genome language models. Using the phage Phi X 174 as a template, the authors generated new phage genomes computationally, then tested them in the lab. They report producing sixteen viable phages with varying fitness levels, and used cryo-electron microscopy to confirm that one generated phage incorporated a DNA packaging protein distinct from its template. The authors also report that a cocktail of these designed phages could overcome strains of E. coli that had become resistant to the original phage, suggesting a possible route toward AI-designed phage therapies against evolving bacterial infections. This peer-reviewed paper has six citations after six weeks, an early but notable proof of concept for designing entire functional genomes rather than single proteins.

Now a cautionary story about integrity in the literature. The outlet 404 Media investigated a company called Research Gold, which markets itself as offering, quote, one hundred percent human-written, never A-I, end quote, medical research services including manuscript drafting and systematic reviews. According to the report, the PhD reviewers the company lists on its website are AI-generated and do not exist, while other real methodologists listed had their names and photos used without permission or knowledge. The reporter found that phone, email, and chat interactions with the company were all handled by AI systems that denied being AI when directly asked. This is investigative journalism, not a scientific study, but it's a striking illustration of how AI-generated content is infiltrating claims of human-verified research. The story drew about one hundred ninety-six points and over fifty comments on Hacker News.

We close with a preprint that generated wide debate. A paper posted to arXiv, in the physics and society category, proposes modeling the spread of large language model use through a viral analogy. The authors describe transitions among what they call uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, and argue that the interplay of social spread, recovery, and reinforcement could produce tipping points toward what they term technological lock-in. They report that their model also identifies conditions for what they call cognitive immunization, meaning ways to reduce dependency and preserve reversibility. This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and its claims are theoretical and model-based rather than drawn from real-world measurement. Still, it drew close to four hundred points and over two hundred fifty comments, reflecting active interest in how AI tools might be reshaping human thinking habits at a population level.

That's your briefing for today. The through-line across these stories is a field moving in two directions at once: AI systems are accelerating discovery in cancer therapy, immunology, and genome design, while also raising new questions about trust, authorship, and cognitive dependence. Thanks for listening, and we'll be back with more tomorrow.
